title: addition and subtraction facts to 20 (developing computational fluency)

lesson.title: Quick Number Facts to Twenty

steps.say: Hi there! Imagine you're at the Saturday farmers market with your family. You pick up eight fresh strawberries, and then your little sister drops five more into the basket. The person at the stand asks, how many altogether? You don't want to count every single berry — you want to just know. That quick knowing is called being fluent with your number facts, and today I'll show you some clever tricks for it.

visual.caption: Eight berries and five more — how many altogether?

steps.say: Here's my favourite trick, and it's called making ten. Ten is a really friendly number, because it's so easy to add to. So instead of counting up five little steps one at a time, we first hop up to ten. We're at eight, and eight needs two more to reach ten. So we take two out of our five, and we jump.

visual.caption: Hop from eight up to the friendly number ten

steps.say: Now, we borrowed two from the five, so there are still three left to add. And this part is easy, because we're standing on ten. Ten plus three is thirteen — you can almost hear it in the word thir-teen. So eight plus five equals thirteen strawberries. We got there in two comfy hops instead of five wobbly ones.

visual.caption: From ten, three more lands on thirteen

steps.say: Here's a second trick, called near doubles. Doubles are facts you probably already know by heart, like seven plus seven is fourteen. So imagine you have seven hockey cards and your friend has eight. Seven plus eight looks new, but look closely — it's just seven plus seven with one extra card sitting beside it. Fourteen, then one more, is fifteen.

visual.caption: Two groups of seven make fourteen, plus one extra makes fifteen

steps.say: Now let's flip it around to subtraction. Say you had sixteen dollars saved up and you spent seven at the bookstore. We can use the friendly ten again, but this time going backwards. From sixteen, hop back six to land right on ten. That's six of the seven dollars used up, so there's just one more to take away. Ten take away one is nine. You have nine dollars left.

visual.caption: Sixteen back to ten, then one more step to nine

steps.say: And here's the loveliest secret of all. Every subtraction fact is really an addition fact wearing a costume. When you see sixteen take away seven, you can just ask yourself, seven plus what makes sixteen? Since you know nine plus seven is sixteen, you already know the answer. Adding and subtracting are two sides of the same coin, so learning one fact actually gives you two.

visual.caption: Both sides weigh the same — that's why the facts are partners

steps.say: So the big idea is this: you don't have to memorize every fact all by itself. You lean on ten, you lean on doubles, and you let addition help you subtract. Pick whichever trick feels comfiest for the numbers in front of you — that's what mathematicians really do. Try one out loud next time you're counting change at the store!

lesson.answer: Make ten, use doubles, and remember that every subtraction fact is just an addition fact in disguise.

practice.question: At the corner store you have fourteen dollars, and you spend six dollars on a bag of BC apples. How much money do you have left? Try hopping back to ten first!
practice.answer: Eight dollars. From fourteen, hop back four to reach ten, then take away the last two: ten take away two is eight. You can also check it with addition, because six plus eight equals fourteen.
